title: Internet Speed Basics: Bandwidth, Upload/Download and Real-World Speed | CialloSpeed
metaDesc: Why does a 300M connection only download at 37MB/s? Why is upload slower than download? Understand bandwidth, rate units, asymmetric links and peak-hour congestion, and read every speed test result correctly.
ogTitle: Internet Speed Basics: Bandwidth, Upload/Download and Real-World Speed
ogDesc: Understand the relationship between bandwidth and real speed, and read your speed test results correctly.
g.h1: Speed Basics: understand every megabit you pay for
g.lead: What's the relationship between your ISP's “300M” and the “37MB/s” in your download manager? Why is upload always slower? This article explains it all in plain words.
g.s1p1: The “100M broadband” your ISP advertises is measured in Mbps (megabits per second), while download software usually shows MB/s (megabytes per second). Since 1 byte = 8 bits, the theoretical conversion divides by 8:
g.s1li1: 100 Mbps line → theoretical peak of about 12.5 MB/s
g.s1li2: 300 Mbps line → theoretical peak of about 37.5 MB/s
g.s1li3: 1000 Mbps (gigabit) → theoretical peak of about 125 MB/s
g.s1p2: Real-world speed also subtracts protocol overhead (TCP/IP headers, the test engine's ~4% compensation factor, etc.), so reaching about 90% of the theoretical value is normal.
g.s2h: 02Why is upload always slower than download?
g.s2p1: Most home broadband uses an asymmetric design: the download channel is far wider than the upload channel. That matches how households actually use the internet — downloading much more than they upload. Typical ratios:
g.s2li1: Ordinary fiber: 300 Mbps down, upload often just 30 Mbps
g.s2li2: Business lines or premium plans: symmetric up/down, at a noticeably higher price
g.s2p2: If you regularly stream live, join video calls or back up to cloud drives, your upload speed deserves a test even more than your download.
g.s3h: 03Slower at peak hours — whose fault is it?
g.s3p1: Slower speeds in the evening peak (20:00–23:00) usually mean shared-bandwidth congestion: everyone in the neighborhood or on the same ISP gateway is online at once, thinning out per-user bandwidth. Other factors can also be at play:
g.s3li1: Aging router: a Wi-Fi 4 router can't saturate a 100M+ connection
g.s3li2: Wi-Fi interference: your neighbor's Wi-Fi channel overlaps with yours
g.s3li3: Cable grade: Cat5 cables top out at 100 Mbps
g.s3li4: Cross-network routing: reaching a server on another carrier's network hits interconnection bottlenecks
g.s3p2: Run a few tests at different times of day and compare. If only the evening peak is slow, it's most likely carrier-side congestion — worth reporting to your ISP.
g.s4p1: Pick a plan based on your household's most demanding activity — no need to overbuy:
g.r3c1: Heavy multi-device home (with NAS / cloud backup)
g.s4p2: For competitive gaming, latency and jitter matter far more than bandwidth.
